In my experience, if you're living a rat race it's usually because you're maintaining something that you shouldn't maintain. Unless you're literally starving, I can guarantee you that there's something you could let go of to free up resources - our psyche is really good at justifying the status quo, but for financial matters it's really important to recognize and tackle the areas where you're bullshitting yourself.

Keep track of your spending patterns. If you notice expenses that aren't vitally important (buying coffee, eating out, recreational drugs, impulse purchases) cut them immediately. Reflect on your situation and figure out if you're actually doing what's most effective for your financial stability. Do you have your current job because it's convenient and comfortable, or because it's the one that makes the most sense financially? What about your living arrangement? Do you really need your own place, or can you cut costs by moving into shared housing? What about your transport costs? Have you actually done the calculations to find out the most cost-effective way to get to work, or are you just maintaining that car because it's convenient and gives you a feeling of independence?

If you've examined all of these things and implement all of your findings in earnest and you're still barely scratching it, go and get a second opinion. Get people who know you to look at your financial situation and give input. There's many cost-cutting measures that can be seen better by an external observer who's not biased towards maintaining the status quo.

Any time you have money left over after all vitally important expenses, use it to pay debt or stash it away. Any time money goes into the stash, you forget that it exists. Then, you do your best, so hopefully by the time shit hits the fan (and it will) the stash will be big enough to avert catastrophe.

it is of vital importance that you budget a small amount for your human luxuries, though. When you go through the trouble to actually plan out your finances, you've earned a little bit for yourself-- $50 a month is more than enough to buy all the junk food, eating out, and random dumb shit you could possibly consume responsibly if you're getting your finances in order.

I get where you're coming from (I'm not very conscientious myself and I have a hedonistic streak, so I'm also budgeting for random dumb shit), but statistically speaking people who have superior self-discipline do better in the long run. Couldn't live like that myself, personally, but the people who generate the most wealth over their lifetime tend to be people who barely spend anything on themselves, work virtually all the time and deliberate every single expense carefully. Psychologically it's related to 'trait conscientiousness', basically a measure of how efficient/organized or easy-going/careless you are. High conscientiousness means high capability for delayed gratification, preference of long-term planning over short-term action, high sense of duty, tenacity when trying to achieve goals and high reliability. Unsurprisingly, it strongly correlates with lifetime earnings, highest degree of education achieved and highest position held while working in the open market.

Sooo, if you're one of the rare persons who can live in absolute financial self-discipline without suffering, then good on you, you'll probably end up making more money than most - but for the rest of us, yeah, a certain amount of luxuries is vital :)

The thing about that is like any other skill, you get better at it the more you do. You learn all of the basics, buying and selling, marketing and logistics, customer service, employee management, counting and accounting, law and taxes, and all the rest. You especially learn about the fraudulent side of human nature - which is something all of us have at least some part of.

It's called entrepreneurship and it is perhaps the best way out of the poverty cycle that exists. America is built on this more than anything else, Canada too.

Fact is, there are only so many ways you can become rich. You can find the money. You can win the money. You can inherit the money. You can steal the money. You can be given the money (especially online.) You can earn the money. If you are working for somebody else when earning your money, it is best to be a skilled individual worthy of a decent paycheck. If you run your own business, then at least you get to write off your expenses, which means you keep more of what you earn. If your business becomes successful, you can earn and keep more money doing that than by any other means.

As an interesting exercise, look at every wealthy person you know and see if you can determine which path they were on that brought them to their wealth. You will see there are really only a few basic ways to get there.

Of course, once you have wealth, you have a whole new set of problems which basically amount to how do you keep it with the entire world trying to take it from you. That's a separate topic for another discussion.

If you do decide to follow the entrepreneur route here is a really good rule of thumb - no matter how good any particular deal sounds, always assume the information is wrong - never enter a deal that if the deal goes bad you are going to be out of business. Mistakes you can recover from - and you'll have plenty no matter how good you are - just do everything you can to avoid the big ones - you get battered and bruised, but you are still in the game. Mistakes that don't kill you make you stronger.
